title: Boulton & Watt: Selling Power
summary: Watt had a great idea but no money, until cheerful Birmingham factory owner Matthew Boulton became his partner. An ironmaster named John Wilkinson made cylinders so round that the steam stopped leaking. Soon their engines were pumping deep mines, and customers paid them a share of all the coal they saved!

sections.heading: A Backer Who Ran Out of Luck
paragraphs: At the end of Part 7 we left James Watt with a patent from 1769, a leaky test engine at Kinneil House in Scotland, and empty pockets. His first backer was John Roebuck, born in Sheffield in 1718, a doctor-turned-industrialist full of big plans. Roebuck had helped start the Carron ironworks near Falkirk in 1759, which became famous for making cast-iron goods and, later, short cannons called carronades. He also leased coal mines and salt works around Bo'ness on the Firth of Forth.

Roebuck's mines had the same problem as so many others in this story: they kept flooding. A pump that used a quarter of the coal of a Newcomen engine sounded like exactly what he needed. In return for paying off Watt's debts and funding experiments, Roebuck took two thirds of the rights to Watt's invention. Watt worked on the engine in a small building behind Kinneil House, Roebuck's home, often travelling back and forth between there and Glasgow.

But the experimental engine would not behave. Its cylinder, made by ordinary methods of the time, was not perfectly round or smooth, so steam leaked past the piston. Watt also had to earn a living, so for several years he spent much of his time surveying routes for canals and harbours in Scotland, tramping through wet fields with measuring chains and instruments. He often felt gloomy about the engine, and in one letter to a friend he grumbled that, of all things in life, nothing was more foolish than inventing.

Then Roebuck's businesses collapsed. His coal mines kept flooding faster than they could be pumped, his debts grew, and in 1773 he went bankrupt. The same year brought sadness for Watt at home: his wife, Margaret Miller, whom he had married in 1764, died, leaving him with two young children. It was one of the hardest times of his life.

Roebuck's creditors, the people he owed money to, looked through his property to see what was worth anything. Watt's patent share was not high on their list; many thought a half-finished engine was nearly worthless. One of those creditors, however, saw things very differently. Roebuck owed him about 1,200 pounds, and he was happy to take Roebuck's share of Watt's patent instead of cash. His name was Matthew Boulton.

sections.heading: Matthew Boulton, Soho and a New Partnership
paragraphs: Matthew Boulton was born in Birmingham on 3 September 1728, the son of a maker of small metal goods. In the 1700s Birmingham was famous for what people called toys. These were not playthings, but small metal articles: shoe buckles, buttons, watch chains, snuff boxes and trinkets. As a teenager Boulton came up with a popular way of inlaying enamel in buckles, and after his father died in 1759 he took over the family business and set out to make it much bigger.

In 1761 Boulton leased about 13 acres of land at Soho, just outside Birmingham, which then lay in Staffordshire. There was a stream, a small rolling mill and a house. He built a grand new factory, the Soho Manufactory, finished by about 1765. Visitors were amazed: a long, handsome building looking more like a country mansion than a workshop, with hundreds of workers inside making buttons, buckles, silver and silver-plated tableware, and decorative gilded ornaments called ormolu. Boulton gathered many processes under one roof and organised the work so that each person did a specialised task, an early example of a modern factory.

Soho was so impressive that it became a tourist attraction for nobles, scientists and foreign visitors, and Boulton loved showing them round. He even set up an insurance scheme for workers in the 1770s, in which employees paid a small part of their wages into a fund that helped them if they were sick or injured. He was cheerful, persuasive, generous with credit and always full of new schemes, almost the opposite of the anxious, careful Watt.

Soho had a weakness, though. Its machines were driven by a waterwheel, and the stream was not strong enough, especially in dry summers. Boulton had already been thinking about using a steam engine to pump water back up above the wheel so it could be reused. That made him very interested indeed when he heard about a Scotsman with a much more economical engine.

Boulton was also a member of the Lunar Society of Birmingham, a group of friends who met once a month on the evening nearest the full moon (so they had moonlight to ride home by) to discuss science and invention. Members included the doctor and poet Erasmus Darwin, the potter Josiah Wedgwood, the chemist Joseph Priestley and the doctor William Small, who had once taught in America. Through these friends Boulton and Watt began writing to each other in 1766 and met in 1768, when Watt passed through Birmingham. They liked each other immediately.

After Roebuck's bankruptcy, Boulton took over his share of the patent. In 1774 Watt packed up and moved to Birmingham, bringing the parts of the Kinneil engine with him. At Soho he had skilled metalworkers, tools, space and, above all, Boulton's money and confidence. In 1775 the two men became partners, and the firm of Boulton and Watt was born. It would last for about 25 years in its first form and then carry on under their sons.

There was a problem with time, though. Watt's 1769 patent would normally last 14 years, until 1783. By 1775 six of those years had already gone, and the engine was still not on the market. Boulton argued that it would take years more to develop and sell the engines, and that without longer protection no one would risk the money. He lobbied Parliament hard, and in 1775 an Act of Parliament extended Watt's patent so that it lasted until 1800. This gave the partners 25 more years in which nobody else in Britain could build an engine with a separate condenser without their permission.

The extension was controversial even then. Some people, including mine owners and rival engineers, argued that it gave one firm too much power over a vital technology. You will see later in this chapter that this argument never really went away.

The partners divided their work in a way that suited their personalities. Watt concentrated on designing, calculating and solving technical problems. Boulton handled money, customers, publicity and politics, and kept the anxious Watt going when he felt like giving up. Watt is often quoted as saying he would rather face a loaded cannon than settle an account or make a bargain. Boulton, in contrast, enjoyed exactly that kind of work. It was a partnership of a brilliant engineer and a brilliant businessman, and the engine needed both.

sections.heading: Iron-Mad Wilkinson and the Perfect Cylinder
paragraphs: The leaking cylinder had defeated Watt in Scotland. The answer came from an ironmaster with a big personality: John Wilkinson, born in 1728, who ran ironworks at Bersham in Wales and at Broseley and Bradley in the English Midlands. People called him Iron-Mad Wilkinson because he wanted to make everything out of iron. He later built an iron barge, helped start the project that became the famous Iron Bridge over the River Severn, and even had an iron coffin made for himself.

In 1774 Wilkinson patented a new way of boring cannon. Before then, cannon were usually cast with a hollow core, and the inside could end up off-centre or uneven, which made guns inaccurate and sometimes dangerous. Wilkinson cast them solid and then bored the hole out by turning the barrel against a cutting tool. The key to his method was that the long bar holding the cutter was firmly supported, so the cutter could not wobble as it moved forward. The result was a straight, round and smooth hole.

A similar machine, with the boring bar supported at both ends, could bore out a large steam engine cylinder. Instead of a wobbly, egg-shaped tube, Watt could now have a cylinder that was truly round all the way along. In 1776 Boulton wrote that a cylinder about 50 inches (about 1.3 metres) across, bored by Wilkinson, did not err the thickness of an old shilling in any part. In other words, along its whole length it was accurate to about the thickness of a thin coin.

That may not sound like much, but it made all the difference. With a cylinder that accurate, a piston packed with materials such as hemp and tallow could fit snugly enough to keep the steam in. The engine that had wheezed at Kinneil was rebuilt at Soho with a Wilkinson cylinder and finally ran well. Many historians call Wilkinson's boring machine one of the first true machine tools, a machine for making other machines precisely. Wilkinson's cannon patent was later overturned in 1779, but he kept a near-exclusive role supplying cylinders to Boulton and Watt for years.

This is an important lesson about invention. Watt's idea was sound in 1765, but it could not succeed until metalworking caught up. Great machines often depend on many other people's tools and skills. A better engine needed a better cylinder, and a better cylinder needed a better boring machine, and that came from the world of making guns.

sections.heading: 1776: The First Engines Go to Work
paragraphs: In 1776 the first Boulton and Watt engines started work. The first, completed in March, was at Bloomfield Colliery, a coal mine at Tipton in the Black Country, west of Birmingham, where it pumped water from the pit. Another, finished about a month later, was at Wilkinson's ironworks near Broseley in Shropshire, where it worked the bellows for a blast furnace, blowing air into the fire to make it hot enough to melt iron ore.

The Bloomfield engine's start was turned into a public event. Imagine a crowd of mine owners, engineers and curious locals standing in the cold around a tall brick engine house, its great beam poking out of the wall. There is a hiss, the beam begins to rock, and, according to accounts of the day, the engine quickly began clearing water from the pit. Local newspapers praised it. Boulton wanted everyone to know that this was a new and better kind of engine.

Interestingly, Boulton and Watt did not at first build entire engines in their own factory. Instead, the firm usually supplied the design drawings, sent skilled men to supervise the building, and provided certain special parts such as valves. The customer bought the heavy parts, like the cylinder from Wilkinson and the beam, from other suppliers, and paid for the engine house. Only in 1795 did the firm open its own engine-making works, the Soho Foundry at Smethwick, which was run mainly by the partners' sons, James Watt Junior and Matthew Robinson Boulton.

1776 was also the year of a famous visit. On a tour of Soho, Boulton showed the writer James Boswell, best known for his biography of Samuel Johnson, around the works. Boswell wrote down what Boulton said to him: "I sell here, Sir, what all the world desires to have, POWER." It was a clever joke, because Soho also sold small luxury items, but it was also true. Boulton understood that he was not only selling a machine; he was selling the ability to do work anywhere, whenever you needed it.

sections.heading: Pay Us a Third of What You Save
paragraphs: How do you sell an expensive new engine to customers who already own old ones? Boulton and Watt came up with an unusual business model. Instead of charging just a fixed price, they asked customers to pay a yearly royalty equal to one third of the value of the coal the new engine saved, compared with a Newcomen engine doing the same work. The payments would continue for the life of the patent, which meant up to 1800.

This was clever. A customer did not have to believe the advertising; they only had to pay if the engine actually saved them money, and they kept two thirds of the savings for themselves. To measure the work, Watt designed a counter, a little clockwork device fixed to the beam that recorded every stroke, so the number of strokes could be checked and the payments calculated. Engineers compared engines using a measure called duty: how many pounds of water an engine could raise one foot high by burning a set amount of coal.

The biggest market was Cornwall, in the far south-west of England. Cornwall's tin and copper mines were some of the deepest in the world, often hundreds of metres down, and they flooded badly. But Cornwall had no coal of its own. Coal had to be shipped in, mostly from South Wales, which made it expensive. For Cornish mine owners, an engine that used about a quarter of the coal was enormously attractive. In the late 1770s the first engines were set up at Cornish mines such as Ting Tang and Wheal Busy near Chacewater, and many more followed. Within a few years, most of the old Newcomen engines in Cornwall had been replaced.

Watt spent long, unhappy months in Cornwall setting up engines and arguing about money. He suffered from headaches and homesickness, and he did not much enjoy the company of the tough, independent Cornish mine captains. To help, the firm relied on a young Scottish engineer, William Murdoch, who joined Boulton and Watt in 1777 and from 1779 was based in Cornwall, managing engine installations and repairs. Murdoch was practical, energetic and inventive, and later in this story he plays a key part in making engines turn wheels.

The royalties soon caused fierce arguments. Some Cornish mine owners felt they were paying too much, year after year, for an idea. When copper prices fell and mines struggled, many simply stopped paying. By the 1790s the firm was owed large sums in Cornwall that it struggled to collect.

sections.heading: A Day at a Cornish Engine House
paragraphs: Let us step into one of those Cornish mines around 1780. On a windy hillside stands a tall, narrow building of granite and slate: the engine house. One thick wall, called the bob wall, carries the weight of the great beam, which sticks out through a high opening above the mine shaft. Beside the engine house rises a brick or stone chimney, trailing coal smoke towards the sea.

Inside, it is warm and noisy. In the boiler house next door, men called stokers shovel coal into the furnace under a large boiler shaped a bit like a wagon roof, which is why it was called a wagon boiler. The steam is not at high pressure; it is only a little above the pressure of the air. A pipe carries it to the cylinder, which stands upright in the engine house, wrapped in its steam jacket and bolted down onto massive stone foundations.

Now watch a stroke. The engineman's valves let steam onto the top of the piston, while underneath it a passage opens to the cold condenser. The steam below the piston rushes into the condenser and vanishes into water, leaving a vacuum. With steam pressing from above and almost nothing pushing back from below, the piston sinks. The beam tilts, and on the outside end, heavy wooden pump rods rise out of the shaft, lifting water up from deep underground through a series of pumps. Then the valves change, steam is allowed to pass to the underside of the piston so pressure on both sides is balanced, and the heavy weight of the pump rods pulls the beam back the other way, ready for the next stroke.

Meanwhile the air pump, driven from the beam, steadily removes the warm water and air from the condenser, and some of that warm water is pumped back into the boiler. A small rod on the beam works the stroke counter, clicking away so the firm can work out the royalty. The engineman's job is to keep the valve gear adjusted, the packing tight and the engine running smoothly, sometimes for weeks at a time without stopping, because if the pumps stop the mine starts to flood.

Hundreds of metres below, miners working by candlelight in the tin and copper lodes depend on this rhythmic rocking for their safety and their jobs. The Cornish engine houses that grew from this period became so typical of the landscape that their ruins are now part of a World Heritage Site, the Cornwall and West Devon Mining Landscape. You will see in Part 11 how later Cornish engineers made these pumping engines even more efficient.

sections.heading: Rivals, Courtrooms and a Fair Question
paragraphs: Cornwall was full of skilled engineers, and some of them built engines of their own that Boulton and Watt said copied their invention. Jonathan Hornblower, from a family of Cornish engineers, designed an engine using two cylinders, an early form of the compound engine you will meet in Part 11. Edward Bull built engines with the cylinder placed upside down directly over the mine shaft, doing away with the beam. Both designs used a separate condenser, and Boulton and Watt took the builders to court.

In the 1790s Boulton and Watt took a series of infringers to court. The cases dragged on through the 1790s and were among the most important patent battles of the age. In the end the courts mostly backed Boulton and Watt, and many of the rival engineers and mine owners settled. The firm still never collected everything it believed it was owed.

Here we must be fair. The strong patent, extended until 1800, protected Watt's years of work and gave Boulton the confidence to invest huge sums before any profit came in. Without that protection, the partnership might never have survived. On the other hand, the patent also slowed down other inventors. Watt himself distrusted high-pressure steam as too dangerous, and while his patent lasted, engineers who wanted to try other ideas involving a condenser risked being sued. Some historians and economists argue that steam technology would have advanced faster without such a long monopoly; others say the patent was what made the business possible. It is a debate about inventions and the law that still goes on today, with medicines, software and much more.

What is certain is that after 1800, when the patent expired, inventors such as Richard Trevithick rushed ahead with new designs, especially high-pressure engines. Watt retired from the business that same year, aged 64, and Boulton left soon after, handing the firm to their sons.

By 1800 Boulton and Watt had built roughly 496 engines, according to commonly quoted figures, for mines, ironworks, breweries, waterworks, cotton mills and many other customers. That number tells a story in itself. In 1775 the separate condenser was a clever idea that had never run properly at full size. Twenty-five years later, Watt engines were at work all across Britain and beyond.

sections.heading: Up and Down Is Not Enough
paragraphs: Let us look again at those very first Boulton and Watt engines at Bloomfield, Broseley and the Cornish mines. They were magnificent, but they all did basically the same thing as Newcomen's engines: the great beam rocked up and down, and pump rods or bellows moved up and down with it. They were pumping engines. They could lift water out of a mine or blow air into a furnace, but they could not easily spin anything.

Yet look at what else was happening in Britain in the 1770s and 1780s. Flour mills ground grain with turning millstones. Cotton mills ran spinning machines on rotating shafts. Ironworks needed rolling mills and hammers driven round and round. Breweries needed pumps and stirrers. Almost every factory machine needed rotary motion, something that turns in a circle, like a wheel. Until now most of that turning came from waterwheels, and in dry summers, as Boulton knew at Soho, the water could run low.

Some mill owners had even tried a strange halfway solution: they used a steam engine to pump water up into a pond, and then let that water run down over a waterwheel to turn the machines. It worked, but it wasted a lot of power. What industry really wanted was a steam engine that could turn a wheel directly, smoothly and steadily, all day long.

Boulton saw the opportunity clearly. He urged Watt to find ways to make the engine turn, and is often quoted as writing that the people in London, Manchester and Birmingham were steam-mill mad. Making an up-and-down engine turn a wheel sounds simple, but it led to a whole series of clever inventions, a patent puzzle, and one of the most ingenious gears ever built. That is the story of the next part.

deepDive: Boulton and Watt's royalty system is one of the earliest examples of charging for a technology by the value it creates rather than by the cost of making it. Customers paid one third of the coal savings compared with a Newcomen engine of the same output, for the remaining life of the patent. To make that work, engineers needed a way to compare engines fairly, and the measure they used was duty: the number of pounds of water raised one foot by burning a fixed quantity of coal (a bushel, roughly 84 pounds or about 38 kilograms). Typical figures quoted by historians are around 5 to 7 million for ordinary Newcomen engines, about 9 to 10 million after John Smeaton's improvements, and around 20 million or more for Watt engines, all approximate because measurements varied widely. Later Cornish engines pushed duty far higher, and in 1811 Cornish engineers began publishing monthly reports of engine performance so mine owners could compare them openly. The patent debate is lively among economists and historians. One side argues the 1775 extension to 1800 was essential: Boulton invested heavily for years before profits arrived, and the firm's survival depended on royalties. The other side, associated for example with economists Michele Boldrin and David Levine, argues that Boulton and Watt spent much effort in courts, that the engine's efficiency barely improved during the final years of the patent, and that the spread of steam power and high-pressure designs sped up after 1800. Both views use real evidence, and the truth may be that the patent helped at first and hindered later. Another useful point is that the engine's success relied on a network of suppliers. Wilkinson's boring machine, Soho's skilled workforce, Murdoch's on-site engineering in Cornwall and the Lunar Society's connections were all part of the system. Roughly 496 engines are commonly said to have been built by the firm between 1775 and 1800, a modest number compared with later decades, but enough to show that steam could be a reliable, saleable product rather than a local experiment.
funFact: John Wilkinson, who bored the cylinders for Boulton and Watt, was so devoted to iron that he had an iron coffin made for himself.
